bull_bear.body:
- Aggressive **inorganic** strategy: Nasmyth (100%, Oct 2025), AS Strategic (51%, Apr 2026), Indrajaal (strategic stake 2023), plus the 2024 reverse-merger into the listed Megasoft shell.
- Dedicated President, Corporate Finance & M&A (ex-Goldman Sachs/UBS). Balance sheet: Equity INR 468 cr, total assets INR 1,059 cr; modest interest (INR 11 cr Q4) implies some leverage. Dividend / buyback policy: not disclosed in deck.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- **Other-Income dependence:** ~38% of FY Total Revenue is Other Income — headline revenue/margins overstate operating quality; watch what this comprises.
- **Acquisition integration:** rapid roll-up (Nasmyth UK, AS Strategic, Indrajaal) + reverse-merger — integration, goodwill, and minority (49% JV / 49% AS Strategic) risks.
- **Disclosure quality (deck):** no YoY comparatives, no segment P&L, no orderbook rupee value, no explicit guidance — typical of a corporate presentation, not a concall.
- **Customer/program concentration:** single-source on many programs (a strength and a concentration risk); ~90% defence orderbook ties revenue to MoD/PSU procurement cycles.
- **FX / cross-border:** UK + European + US operations introduce GBP/EUR/USD exposure; tariff/export-control risk on NATO/defence work.
- **Stale public classification:** still tagged as a telecom (Megasoft) name in metadata — index/screen mis-tagging risk.

bull_bear.body:
- The "₹413 Cr Revenue (Q4 FY26)" hero number on slide 4 **includes ~INR 91 cr Other Income**; true operating revenue is INR 323 cr (Q4) / INR 492 cr (FY) — the single most important adjustment for anyone modelling this name.
- This is functionally a **brand-new listed A&D vehicle wearing an old telecom (Megasoft) listing** — screeners, indices and metadata still mis-classify it as Telecom; the real comparable set is defence-electronics / aero-components names.
- The differentiated asset is **Nasmyth's Delegatory Approvals**, which let Sigma legally fast-track transfer of UK aero-engine/airframe work to its low-cost Sri City SEZ — the crux of the margin-expansion thesis (verify execution next quarter).
- ~90% international orderbook + 85% international revenue makes this an unusually **export-tilted** Indian defence name (most peers are domestic-MoD-led).

business.body:
- [Corporate structure] Sigma Advanced Systems and its subsidiaries were approved for merger with the listed entity (formerly Megasoft) effective April 2024, so the current listed vehicle is a post-merger platform.
- [Policy tailwind] India is the world's fifth-largest defence spender but second-largest importer; defence spend at ~1.9% of GDP is near record lows, with capital outlay expected to rise 6.5x over FY25E to USD 122bn by FY47E.
- [Indigenisation] MoD has notified five indigenisation lists covering 5,012 items with 3,002 already indigenised, leaving processed materials (titanium, specialty alloys) still import-dependent and open as opportunity.
- [Market backdrop] Global aerospace market is projected to roughly double from USD 402.8bn (2025) to USD 846.3bn by 2035 at ~7.7% CAGR, with MRO and space adjacencies expanding the TAM.
- [Leadership] Board and KMP are built around sectoral depth - a former Vice Chief of the Indian Army Staff as independent director, ex-Nasmyth COO running international operations, and an ex-Goldman Sachs/UBS executive heading corporate finance and M&A.

outlook.body: Sigma is building a manufacturing network across India and the UK, stated as 300,000+ sq. ft. of manufacturing infrastructure across eight locations. Indian sites: Hyderabad (defence R&D, engineering, manufacturing, testing and quality campus) and Bangalore (precision machining). UK network sites: Bulwell (advanced machining), GEB (surface treatment), Henton (larger components), Coventry (precision fabrication), Ferndown (fabrication, welding, machining, assembly) and IEC (downstream assembly and machining). The next stage of Indian expansion is Sri City, a purpose-built aerospace facility for global-standard manufacturing at scale. It is meant to receive qualified programmes transferred from the UK, and the indicative transfer timeline for qualified work into India is 4-6 months. Footprint and capability were also added through acquisitions: Nasmyth (UK aerospace manufacturing), AS Strategic (European defence market access) and Bromford. This bundle gives no commissioning date for Sri City.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Around 75% of India's capital acquisition budget (Rs. 1.39 lakh crore) is reserved for domestic defence industries in FY2026-27, protecting order pipelines for platform makers and their sub-system and component suppliers.
- Global aerospace demand is running ahead of capacity: the commercial aircraft backlog reached nearly 15,000 units in 2025, and supply-chain performance and workforce capacity are the binding constraints.
- Defence backlog has grown more than 50% over three years as conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East push procurement to record levels.
- OEMs are prioritising supply-chain sovereignty, supplier diversification and dual sourcing away from single-source and single-geography dependencies.
- Customs duty exemptions on aircraft components and MRO raw materials in the Union Budget 2026-27 lower the landed cost of localising aerospace work in India.
- Indian private players are forming JVs with global OEMs to move from parts supply to co-developed sub-systems, opening access to NATO-aligned and European programmes.
- Counter-drone demand is growing fast, with the India counter-drone segment growing at about 28% a year through 2030.
- Execution and capacity, not demand, are described as the sector's binding constraint, so credible capacity expansion converts more directly into revenue growth.
- Order book of Rs. 8,000 crore as on April 2026; ~75% linked to aerospace, and ~66% of the aerospace order book is in the complex aero-engine segment.
- At the end of Q1 FY27: aerospace order book of about Rs. 6,300 crore to be executed over approximately 7 years, a defence export order book of about Rs. 1,400 crore and a defence electronics order book of about Rs. 250 crore.
- Management describes the order book as the foundation for a first revenue milestone of Rs. 5,000 crore.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Around 75% of India's capital acquisition budget (Rs. 1.39 lakh crore) is reserved for domestic defence industries in FY2026-27, protecting order pipelines for platform makers and their sub-system and component suppliers.
- Global aerospace demand is running ahead of capacity: the commercial aircraft backlog reached nearly 15,000 units in 2025, and supply-chain performance and workforce capacity are the binding constraints.
- Defence backlog has grown more than 50% over three years as conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East push procurement to record levels.
- OEMs are prioritising supply-chain sovereignty, supplier diversification and dual sourcing away from single-source and single-geography dependencies.
- Customs duty exemptions on aircraft components and MRO raw materials in the Union Budget 2026-27 lower the landed cost of localising aerospace work in India.
- Indian private players are forming JVs with global OEMs to move from parts supply to co-developed sub-systems, opening access to NATO-aligned and European programmes.
- Counter-drone demand is growing fast, with the India counter-drone segment growing at about 28% a year through 2030.
- Execution and capacity, not demand, are described as the sector's binding constraint, so credible capacity expansion converts more directly into revenue growth.
- Order book of Rs. 8,000 crore as on April 2026; ~75% linked to aerospace, and ~66% of the aerospace order book is in the complex aero-engine segment.
- At the end of Q1 FY27: aerospace order book of about Rs. 6,300 crore to be executed over approximately 7 years, a defence export order book of about Rs. 1,400 crore and a defence electronics order book of about Rs. 250 crore.
- Management describes the order book as the foundation for a first revenue milestone of Rs. 5,000 crore.

UK network sites: Bulwell (advanced machining), GEB (surface treatment), Henton (larger components), Coventry (precision fabrication), Ferndown (fabrication, welding, machining, assembly) and IEC (downstream assembly and machining).
